title: Was it natural? Rome's three senses of natural: from birth, agreeable to nature, flowing from nature's principles
source_text: III. Quaeritur autem an ista justitia & sanctitas primo homini fuerit naturalis, necne? Ad quam quaestionem ut respondeant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, observant naturale variis modis sumi. Primo enim naturale dicitur omne quod habetur a nativitate: & ita naturale opponitur adventitio. Secundo naturale vocatur illud quod est naturae consentaneum, quodque naturam non destruit, sed potius ornat & perficit. Quo sensu naturale opponitur ei quod est contra naturam. Tertio naturale vocatur quod aut est pars naturae, aut fluit ex principiis naturae, vel ab illis fluere aptum est. Qua significatione corpus & animus, facultates quoque tum sentiendi, tum intelligendi, & operationes quae ab eis facultatibus, absque auxilio naturam superante exercentur, naturalia dicuntur: & ita naturale opponitur supernaturali.
pass_a_gloss: But it is asked whether that justice and sanctity was natural to the first man, or not? To answer this question the Doctors of the Roman Church observe that natural is taken in various ways. For first natural is called everything which is had from birth: and so natural is opposed to adventitious. Second that is called natural which is agreeable to nature, and which does not destroy nature, but rather adorns and perfects it. In which sense natural is opposed to that which is against nature. Third that is called natural which either is part of nature, or flows from the principles of nature, or is apt to flow from them. In which signification body and soul, also the faculties both of sensing and of understanding, and the operations which are exercised by those faculties without aid surpassing nature, are called natural: and so natural is opposed to supernatural.
pass_b_english: The question is whether this righteousness and holiness was natural to the first man or not. To answer it, the teachers of the Roman Church point out that "natural" is used in several ways.

First, whatever one has from birth is called natural, and in this sense natural is opposed to acquired. Second, what suits nature, what does not destroy nature but rather adorns and perfects it, is called natural; in this sense natural is opposed to what is against nature.

Third, what is either a part of nature, or flows from nature's principles, or is fitted to flow from them, is called natural. In this sense the body and the soul, the powers of sense and of understanding, and the acts those powers perform without help that goes beyond nature, are called natural, and so natural is opposed to supernatural.

choices.why: Adventitium is what comes to a thing from outside after its origin; 'acquired' carries that in plain English.
